title: Come and see
hookLine: many practice without taking refuge; the teaching invites you to come and see
carry: the lamp shows, the seeing is yours

cards: There's a certain kind of cook who, when you ask what's in the soup, doesn't explain. She just hands you a spoon. Don't take my word for it.
Taste. It's a confident move: it only works if the soup is good. This week has been about practicing with people: a sangha, a friend, a temple, maybe taking refuge someday.
But plenty of people practice for years without any of that, and the teaching doesn't check anyone's ID at the door. It hands you a spoon.

teach.b: In Theravada temples and homes, people chant a short list of the qualities of the Buddha's teaching. In Pali it begins: "Svākkhāto bhagavatā dhammo, sandiṭṭhiko, akāliko, ehipassiko."
In plain English: the teaching is well spoken by the Blessed One, visible here and now, not a matter of time, and ehipassiko.
Ehi means come. Passa means see. It's a word made from an invitation: the teaching is the come-and-see kind.
Not come and believe. Not come and sign. The same list goes on to say it leads onward, and that the wise know it for themselves.
You heard that spirit with the Kalamas, too: test it yourself.

teach.h: A LAMP HELD UP IN THE DARK.
teach.b: And in the old discourses, a listener often ends by saying something like: it's as if you set upright what was overturned, or held up a lamp in the dark so those with eyes could see. The lamp shows. The seeing is yours.
That's one reason people can practice without any label. Some take refuge and some never do.

Some come through a temple, some through a library book or an app like this one. The invitation doesn't change. So this stretch of the path, about practicing alongside other people, closes on an open door.
Tomorrow the big lookout begins: six days to look back at the whole year, starting with the stories.

how: Theravada Buddhists chant the qualities of the Dhamma, including ehipassiko, in their devotions; teachers across traditions welcome people to practice without taking refuge or calling themselves Buddhist.

o: go forth and share the teaching widely
a chant asking the Buddha for protection
come and see: look for yourself first

games.q: match the qualities of the teaching.

s: it means come and see: the teaching is the kind you look at for yourself.
Theravada chanting includes the qualities of the teaching
you must take refuge before you're allowed to practice
many practice for years without any label; the invitation doesn't change.

games.q: a friend is curious about meditation but says, I'm not Buddhist and don't want to be. what does ehipassiko suggest you say?
o: you don't need a label; try it and see what it does.
games.why: the teaching calls itself the come-and-see kind: it invites looking, not signing up.

practice: For this sit, drop every label: you're not a Buddhist or a non-Buddhist, just someone breathing and seeing what's here.
Watch one breath all the way in and all the way out, and ask whether watching brings a little more ease, or not. Don't decide in advance; come and see.

wordCard.voice: Ehipassiko. Come and see: the teaching invites you to look for yourself, not to believe first.

orig.note: Pali ehipassiko: from ehi (come) + passa (see): the come-and-see kind.

carryVoice: Your line: the lamp shows, the seeing is yours. No label required. That's day three hundred twenty-five.

sources.ref: Dhammanussati (the recollection of the Dhamma), e.g. Anguttara Nikaya 11.12
